questions.stem: Which of the following best defines consumer surplus?
options: The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay
The total amount consumers spend on a good
The profit a firm makes on each sale
The excess supply of a good in a market
questions.why: Globalisation raises consumer surplus by lowering prices through imports, competition and economies of scale.
whyNot: That is consumer expenditure.
That is producer surplus or profit.
That is a surplus of output, not consumer surplus.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a benefit of globalisation named in the specification?
options: Lower prices and higher consumer surplus
Higher income inequality within countries
Displaced workers in import-competing industries
Loss of tax revenue from transfer pricing
questions.why: The six named benefits are growth, tax revenue, economies of scale, lower prices and consumer surplus, more choice, and higher living standards.
whyNot: That is a named cost.
That is a named cost.
That is a named cost.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a cost of globalisation named in the specification?
options: The influence of TNCs on domestic economic policy
Increased economic growth
Wider consumer choice
Economies of scale for producers
questions.why: The six named costs are displaced workers, exploitation, environmental impact, lost tax revenue, higher inequality within countries, and TNC influence on policy.
whyNot: That is a named benefit.
That is a named benefit.
That is a named benefit.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines structural unemployment?
options: Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the jobs available
Unemployment caused by a fall in aggregate demand during a recession
Unemployment caused by workers moving between jobs
Unemployment caused by seasonal changes in demand
questions.why: It is what displaced workers experience after a shift in the pattern of trade, and it persists because the mismatch is not quickly resolved.
whyNot: That is cyclical unemployment.
That is frictional unemployment.
That is seasonal unemployment.

questions.stem: Why can globalisation raise output without raising the price level?
options: It shifts aggregate supply to the right as well as aggregate demand
It reduces aggregate demand while raising aggregate supply
It has no effect on aggregate demand
It fixes prices through international agreement
questions.why: Investment, technology and cheaper imported inputs raise productive capacity, which is why the decades of fastest integration combined growth with low inflation.
whyNot: It raises AD through exports and investment.
Exports and FDI both raise AD directly.
Prices are not fixed by agreement.

questions.stem: Why do lower import prices benefit low-income households most in proportional terms?
options: They spend a larger share of their income on traded goods such as clothing and food
They receive a direct subsidy from importers
They buy a greater absolute quantity of imports
They pay no indirect taxes on imports
questions.why: This partly offsets the inequality criticism of globalisation and is frequently missed in essays.
whyNot: No such subsidy exists.
Higher-income households buy more in absolute terms.
They pay the same indirect taxes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines transfer pricing?
options: Setting the prices at which parts of the same company trade with each other
Charging different prices in different countries
Transferring ownership of a firm to a foreign buyer
The price paid for a transfer of government assets
questions.why: It allows a company to report costs in high-tax countries and profits in low-tax ones, reducing tax revenue.
whyNot: That is price discrimination.
That is an acquisition.
That is a privatisation receipt.

questions.stem: Why is the environmental impact of increased trade described as a negative externality?
options: The cost falls on third parties and is not reflected in the price, so the market over-produces
The cost is paid entirely by the producer
The cost is recorded in the balance of payments
The cost only arises in developed economies
questions.why: Emissions from shipping, relocation to weaker regulatory regimes and resource depletion are all unpriced costs.
whyNot: If the producer paid it, it would be an internal cost, not an externality.
Environmental costs are not recorded there.
They arise wherever production and transport occur.

questions.stem: Why is the tax revenue effect of globalisation described as uncertain?
options: Higher output widens the tax base while transfer pricing and tax competition reduce receipts
Tax revenue cannot be measured accurately
Globalisation has no effect on output
Tax rates are fixed by international agreement
questions.why: The benefit and the cost work against each other, which is why the net effect is genuinely uncertain.
whyNot: Revenue is measured routinely.
It raises output substantially.
Rates are set nationally, and competition has driven them down.

questions.stem: Which statement about globalisation and inequality is correct?
options: Inequality between countries has fallen while inequality within many countries has risen
Inequality has risen both between and within countries
Inequality has fallen both between and within countries
Globalisation has had no measurable effect on inequality
questions.why: Fast growth in Asia narrowed the gap between countries, while lower-skilled workers in developed economies lost ground within them.
whyNot: Between-country inequality has fallen.
Within-country inequality has risen in many economies.
The effects are large and well documented.

questions.stem: Why does the political reaction against globalisation exceed its measured aggregate cost?
options: The gains are spread thinly while the losses are concentrated in particular industries and regions
The aggregate cost has been understated in all official data
Consumers do not benefit from trade at all
Total output falls as a result of trade
questions.why: Concentrated losses are visible and organised; diffuse gains are not, which is the central political economy point.
whyNot: The issue is distribution rather than measurement.
Consumers gain through lower prices and choice.
Total output rises.

questions.stem: What is the standard policy conclusion of a balanced essay on globalisation?
options: Compensate and retrain the losers rather than reverse the integration
Reverse the integration through tariffs and capital controls
Do nothing, because the aggregate gains are positive
Subsidise the industries that have lost competitiveness indefinitely
questions.why: Education and training, regional policy and the tax and benefit system address the distribution without giving up the efficiency gains.
whyNot: Reversal would give up the aggregate gains.
Doing nothing ignores the concentrated losses.
Permanent subsidy delays adjustment at continuing cost.

questions.stem: What is the counter-argument to the claim that globalisation exploits workers in developing countries?
options: Wages in export sectors are frequently above the local average, and the local alternative is often worse
Working conditions in export sectors are always excellent
No workers in developing countries are employed by exporters
Exploitation is impossible where wages are paid in cash
questions.why: The response to that counter-argument is that the local alternative is not the only relevant standard, and safety and child labour are not matters of local preference.
whyNot: Conditions are often poor by international standards.
Export sectors are major employers.
The form of payment is irrelevant.

questions.stem: Which of the following explains how economies of scale arise from globalisation?
options: Firms serving world rather than national markets spread fixed costs over greater volume
Firms reduce their output to raise prices
Governments subsidise exporters to lower their costs
Firms merge with their suppliers to avoid tax
questions.why: Lower long-run average cost then lowers prices and improves competitiveness.
whyNot: Lower output raises unit costs.
Subsidy is not the same as a scale economy.
Vertical integration is a different mechanism.

questions.stem: Which structure produces the strongest essay on the effects of globalisation?
options: Separate the efficiency question from the distribution question
List all six benefits and then all six costs
Discuss only the effects on consumers
Argue that the effects cannot be judged
questions.why: On efficiency there is little dispute; the disputes are about distribution, and that structure produces a genuine judgement rather than a verdict.
whyNot: An unweighted list caps the marks at the lower bands.
Consumers are one group among several.
The effects are extensively documented and can be judged.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a race to the bottom?
options: Competition between countries to attract investment by lowering labour, tax or environmental standards
Competition between firms to charge the lowest price
A fall in a currency's value against others
A decline in a country's GDP per capita
questions.why: Each government's action is individually rational and all end up worse off, which is a collective action problem.
whyNot: That is price competition.
That is depreciation.
That is falling income per head.
